C1 alone establishes the association between the Kestrel/Faulk exposure and resignation (R1 and R2 move from unknown to association-only). It also shows the two exposures coincide perfectly, which keeps H2 and H3 unknown. Every other plausible request is deliberately non-discriminating. C4 has no heavy-hours team without Faulk. C6 gives split reasons. C5 and C14 are interested or mention both factors. C3, C9 and C15 are blind to matter. C12 confirms Faulk leads both phases. A3 and A4 are each tied to one live hypothesis and are reversible, so they are premature. The January 2027 phase change stops either of them working as a clean test. case.title: Associate departures from a regulatory investigations group
case.setting: Ferrand Hale LLP is a fictional mid-size London law firm. Its Regulatory Investigations practice group had 24 associates on 1 October 2025. In the following twelve months nine of them resigned. In October 2025 a lateral partner, Dorian Faulk, joined the group, and the group won 'Kestrel', its largest matter so far: a regulator-ordered review for Halvergate Bank. The managing partner, the group head and the associates each explain the departures differently.
case.presentingRequest: The management committee has postponed its decision and asked you to say what is driving the associate departures in Regulatory Investigations and what the firm should do next. Three interventions have been proposed, and the managing partner wants to announce a retention payment this month and close the review.

initialEvidence.source: Email from Graham Teversham, Managing Partner, to the management committee, 29 September 2026
initialEvidence.text: Colleagues — we have now lost nine associates from Regulatory Investigations in twelve months. I've spoken to two recruiters and the picture is clear: Brennick & Stowe are paying around £15k more at three years' qualification, and our people know it. Seven of the nine exit forms give 'career opportunity' as the reason, which in my experience means money. The January billable-target change applies to every group, so it can't explain one group. I propose a £12k retention payment for every associate in the group, announced this month, after which I'd like us to close this review and move on. — GT

initialEvidence.source: HR attrition report, 12 months to 30 September 2026
initialEvidence.text: Voluntary associate resignations, 1 Oct 2025 – 30 Sep 2026. Regulatory Investigations: 9 resignations against an opening headcount of 24 (37.5%); prior year 3 of 23 (13.0%). Other groups: Corporate 12.1% (prior year 13.4%); Banking 14.0% (12.8%); Disputes 11.5% (12.2%); Real Estate 13.3% (14.1%). Regulatory Investigations resignations by month: Dec 2025 (1), Feb 2026 (2), Mar (1), May (2), Jun (1), Aug (1), Sep (1). The firm-wide associate billable target rose from 1,900 to 2,000 hours from 1 January 2026, for all groups. This report does not record matter assignment or supervising partner.

initialEvidence.source: Memo from Priya Lindqvist, head of Regulatory Investigations, 2 October 2026
initialEvidence.text: Two things changed in October 2025. Dorian Faulk joined us as a partner from another firm, and we won the Kestrel mandate, a regulator-ordered review of complaints handling for Halvergate Bank and the largest matter this group has run. At its peak Kestrel had 11 associates. The document-review phase runs to the end of December 2026. From January 2027 the matter moves to report drafting with four associates. Big investigations are hard on juniors; that is the nature of the work. Dorian brought Kestrel in and is exactly the partner this group needed. I would resist any account that makes this about him.

initialEvidence.source: Regulatory Investigations associate pulse survey, July 2026 (15 of 20 responded)
initialEvidence.text: Scores out of 5, with the firm-wide average in brackets: 'My workload is sustainable' 2.3 (3.4). 'The partners I work for treat me with respect' 2.8 (3.9). 'I get useful feedback on my work' 2.9 (3.6). 'I am fairly paid relative to the market' 3.0 (new item; no firm comparison). Selected free-text comments: 'Months of weekends on the investigation. Nobody can keep this up.' — 'Drafts come back after midnight with corrections copied to the whole team. It's humiliating.' — 'Rival firms pay more for less.' — 'I'd stay if I could get off the big matter.' The survey tool does not record which matters respondents work on.

Item 4, Regulatory Investigations attrition. The committee agreed to postpone a decision until the analysis is done. Options tabled: (a) a £12k retention payment for every associate in the group (GT), estimated cost £228k across 19 associates; (b) contract reviewers to take over Kestrel first-level review, about £160k absorbed by the firm because the client will not fund it (PL); (c) moving supervision of Kestrel associates to another partner (associate representative). HR reported that an external interviewer could hold confidential interviews with departed and current associates within three weeks for about £9k. Four of the nine leavers have already agreed to take part. Action: analyst to recommend.

catalogue.title: Associate matter-assignment and supervising-partner records with departure dates, Oct 2025 – Sep 2026
catalogue.source: Practice management system export, Regulatory Investigations
catalogue.text: The export covers the 24 associates in the group on 1 October 2025. The four lateral hires since then are excluded, and none of them has resigned. Kestrel: 11 associates were assigned between October 2025 and January 2026, with a PQE spread of 1–6 years, similar to the group as a whole. All 11 are recorded with Dorian Faulk as supervising partner. Faulk is recorded on no other matter carrying associate time, and no associate recorded Kestrel time under any other partner. Resigned: 8 of the 11 Kestrel associates (median seven months after joining the team) and 1 of the 13 associates never assigned to Kestrel. Staffing note: Kestrel places were filled from the associates with the lowest forward utilisation in October 2025.

catalogue.title: Salary benchmarking and leaver destination records, 2026
catalogue.source: HR reward team and departure records
catalogue.text: Base salaries against the 2026 external legal salary survey (London, mid-size firms): Regulatory Investigations associates sit at the 54th–61st percentile at every PQE level, the same band as the rest of the firm. 2026 bonuses were paid at the firm standard. Where the nine leavers went: in-house legal teams 4, the regulator 2, other law firms 2 (one to Brennick & Stowe at +£4k base, one to a similar firm at equal base), career break 1. Of the 8 leavers whose new salary is known, 6 took equal or lower base pay. Brennick & Stowe's published band at 3 PQE is £3–5k above Ferrand Hale's, not £15k.

catalogue.title: HR exit-interview forms for the nine leavers
catalogue.text: Standard tick-box form, completed with the HR business partner. Primary reason: 'Career opportunity' 7, 'Work–life balance' 1, 'Personal' 1. Free-text box: five left blank. The others read 'Time for something new', 'Good opportunity came up', 'Thanks to everyone for the support' and 'Wanted a change of pace'. No form records the leaver's matter or supervising partner. HR note: leavers are told the form may be placed on file and seen by the practice group head.

catalogue.title: Recorded hours by matter team, Oct 2025 – Sep 2026
catalogue.text: Average annualised recorded hours per associate. Kestrel team: 2,270, with weekend time entries on 31% of weekends. All other Regulatory Investigations matters combined: 1,940, with weekend entries on 6% of weekends. Firm-wide associate average: 1,920. No other matter team in the group averaged above 2,050. Timekeeping note: the supervising partner reviewed Kestrel time entries weekly before billing, and some associates say they under-recorded late-night drafting time.

catalogue.title: Interview with Dorian Faulk, partner, 8 October 2026
catalogue.text: Kestrel has deadlines set by the regulator. The client can't move them and neither can I. Yes, I send comments late. That's when I get to the drafts, because I'm in client meetings all day. I copy the team so everyone learns from the corrections; that's how I was trained. I asked for three more associates in March and was told no. Put any partner on this matter with eleven associates and you'd see the same strain. My last firm's team ran investigations like this and people progressed well.

catalogue.title: Interview with the group's staffing coordinator, 9 October 2026
catalogue.text: I assign by availability. Nobody made a formal request to leave Kestrel. People don't, because it looks bad. Informally, four came to me asking whether they could rotate off 'the investigation'. When I asked why, one said 'the hours', one said 'Dorian', one said 'all of it', and one wouldn't say. I couldn't move anyone, because Kestrel needed the numbers and there was no other partner on that matter to put them under. I honestly don't know which of those things pushed people out.

catalogue.title: Reference letter from Dorian Faulk's former firm, August 2025
catalogue.text: Dorian led our financial crime investigations practice for six years and delivered several of the largest mandates in the market. He is exacting and holds his teams to a high standard. Clients trust him completely. We were sorry to see him go and recommend him without reservation to any firm building an investigations capability.

catalogue.title: Firm billable-target policy memo, December 2025
catalogue.text: From 1 January 2026 the annual billable target for all associates rises from 1,900 to 2,000 hours. Bonus eligibility still requires 95% of target. Group heads may apply for target relief for associates on secondment or extended leave. The change applies in the same way to every practice group, and no group-specific variations will be granted.

catalogue.title: Regulatory Investigations pulse survey scores by PQE band, July 2026
catalogue.text: 'Workload sustainable': 1–2 PQE 2.4; 3–4 PQE 2.2; 5+ PQE 2.4. 'Partners treat me with respect': 2.9; 2.7; 2.8. 'Fairly paid': 3.1; 2.9; 3.0. The survey tool merges any band with fewer than five responses. To protect anonymity it does not collect matter or supervising partner, so scores cannot be split by team.

catalogue.title: Client feedback on Kestrel from Halvergate Bank, September 2026
catalogue.text: The Ferrand Hale team has been responsive under very tight regulator deadlines. The interim findings were of high quality and well evidenced. Billing has been in line with the capped fee. We would welcome Ferrand Hale continuing into the reporting phase and would consider the firm for future regulatory work.

catalogue.title: Legal recruiter market report: associate mobility, 2026
catalogue.text: Across mid-size London firms, associate voluntary attrition was 14% in 2026, against 15% in 2025. In-house demand for regulatory lawyers rose modestly over the year. Movement to regulators was in line with prior years. The report does not break its data down by firm or practice group.

catalogue.title: Kestrel engagement letter and project plan
catalogue.text: Phase 1 (Oct 2025 – Dec 2026): document review and interviews, with a planned associate complement of 9–11. Phase 2 (Jan – Jun 2027): report drafting, with a planned complement of 4. Dorian Faulk is named as relationship and supervising partner for both phases. Fees are capped. Contract reviewer costs outside the cap need the client's written consent, which the client declined in May 2026.

catalogue.title: Facilities record: floor moves, 2026
catalogue.text: In February 2026 floor 5 (Regulatory Investigations, Disputes and Real Estate) was converted to open-plan seating with hot-desking for associates. Attrition in Disputes and Real Estate is within one percentage point of the prior year. A post-move occupant survey rated the new space 3.6 out of 5.

catalogue.title: Email exchange between Dorian Faulk and Priya Lindqvist, March 2026
catalogue.text: DF: 'Kestrel needs three more associates. The team is stretched and I'm covering the gaps by keeping people late. That isn't sustainable.' PL: 'I can't release anyone else without hurting other clients. Can you phase the review?' DF: 'The regulator sets the phases. We'll manage.' PL: 'Understood. Please keep an eye on morale.'

catalogue.title: Farewell emails sent by departing associates
catalogue.text: Nine farewell emails were sent to the group distribution list. All thank colleagues warmly. None gives a reason for leaving or names a matter or partner. Typical text: 'It's been a privilege to work with such talented people. I'm off to a new challenge and will miss you all. Do stay in touch.'

hypotheses.text: Pay below what competing firms offer is driving the group's associates to resign.
The supervisory practices of the partner who joined the group in October 2025 are driving associates to resign.
The volume and nature of the work on the large investigation matter won in October 2025 are driving associates to resign.
The firm-wide increase in the associate billable-hours target is driving the group's associates to resign.
The group's resignations reflect ordinary market-wide associate mobility rather than anything specific to the group.

edges.from: Supervision by the partner who joined in October 2025
Assignment to the review workload of the large investigation matter

actions.text: Commission confidential interviews with departed and current Kestrel associates, run by an interviewer outside the group's reporting lines and structured to separate experiences of supervision from experiences of workload, before choosing an intervention.
Pay a group-wide retention payment matching the rival firm's quoted pay and close the attrition review as resolved.
Move day-to-day supervision of Kestrel associates from the partner who joined in October 2025 to another partner for the rest of the matter.
Bring in a firm-funded contract review team to take over first-level document review on Kestrel for the rest of the review phase.
Add matter and supervising-partner fields to the firm's attrition reporting and track them monthly from now on.

truth.groundTruthNarrative: The surge in departures is specific to the group and sits inside the Kestrel team. Eight of the 11 Kestrel associates resigned, against 1 of the 13 associates who never worked on Kestrel. Pay is not the driver: the group's salaries sit at the 54th–61st percentile, the same as the rest of the firm. Six of the eight leavers with a known new salary took equal or lower base pay, and the rival firm's real premium is £3–5k, not the £15k the managing partner cited. The billable-target rise was firm-wide and took effect after the first resignation, and attrition in other groups did not move. Market-wide mobility was flat. What the evidence cannot settle is whether associates left because of the new partner's supervision, because of Kestrel's heavy review workload, or both. The two exposures coincide completely: every Kestrel associate was supervised by Faulk, Faulk supervised no associate outside Kestrel, and no other team ran comparable hours. Every other source is either interested (Faulk, the group head) or blind to matter (the survey, exit forms and farewell emails), or it mentions both factors (the coordinator, the emails). Confidential, structured interviews that separate supervision from workload are the best next step. Committing now to a supervision change or contract reviewers would be a bet on an unestablished hypothesis, and a retention payment followed by closing the review would be harmful.

answers.rationale: The managing partner's £15k claim, the 'career opportunity' tick-boxes and a survey comment all point to pay. C2 shows pay at the 54th–61st percentile, in line with the rest of the firm, which is not losing people. Six of the eight leavers with a known new salary took equal or lower base pay, and the rival's real premium is £3–5k. This counts against the claim.

Vivid survey comments about midnight corrections tempt 'supported'. But C1 shows that supervision by Faulk and assignment to Kestrel are the same set of associates, so departures covary with both equally. No item separates them: the coordinator's answers are split, Faulk's and the group head's accounts are interested, and the survey and exit records do not record matter or partner. The claim is live but not established.

The group head and Faulk attribute the departures to the matter, and C4 shows Kestrel's very high hours. But C4 reports no other heavy-hours team without Faulk, and C1 shows no Kestrel associate who worked under a different partner. The workload explanation therefore cannot be separated from the supervision explanation. Both stay unknown.

The target rise applied to every group from January 2026, and attrition in other groups stayed at prior-year levels. The group's first resignation came in December 2025, before the change. C1 adds that non-Kestrel associates in the same group, under the same target, left at 1 in 13.
The group's rate rose from 13% to 37.5% while every other group and the external market (C11) were flat or slightly down. The pattern is specific to the group, not market-wide.

C1 shows that supervision by Faulk co-occurs with resignation (8 of 11 against 1 of 13), and the onset fits the timing. However, the rival exposure (Kestrel's workload) applies to exactly the same associates, and assignment by low utilisation adds a selection rival. Causation is not established. Without C1 not even the association is visible.

Kestrel assignment covaries strongly with resignation (C1), and C4 shows a plausible heavy-hours mechanism. But supervision by Faulk is perfectly confounded with it, so the link is an association only.
The link itself fails: pay is not below market, most leavers accepted equal or lower pay, and the same pay bands firm-wide go with normal attrition.
A firm-wide change cannot account for an increase confined to one group when other groups under the same change were unaffected. The increase also began before the change took effect.

The two live explanations cannot be separated from existing records. Confidential interviews outside the reporting line are cheap (£9k) and fast (three weeks), and four leavers have already agreed to take part. They are the only available route to separating supervision from workload, and existing channels (exit forms seen by the group head, a survey with no matter field) suppress that signal.

The pay hypothesis is contradicted. Whether the driver is supervision or workload, £228k goes to the wrong lever, and closing the review halts the investigation while the Kestrel team keeps losing people. This worsens outcomes under every live hypothesis.

If supervision were confirmed as the driver, this would clearly help, and it is reversible because only day-to-day supervision moves. But that hypothesis is unestablished. Workload also drops in January 2027 (E3), so any improvement afterwards would not even show whether the move worked.

If workload were confirmed as the driver this would help, and its cost of about £160k causes no lasting damage. But the workload explanation is not established over the supervision explanation. The review phase also ends in December 2026, so the firm would be spending money on an unconfirmed bet.

It is reasonable and fixes a real gap: E2 records neither matter nor partner. But it is slow, and on Kestrel's current staffing it cannot separate the two explanations, because supervisor and matter coincide completely. So it is not the best next action.

Pay, the billable target and market mobility are ruled out, but each substantive intervention (A3, A4) depends on a hypothesis the evidence cannot separate from its rival. Doing nothing is not warranted, because the attrition is real and concentrated in one team.

truth.authoringNotes: Design: three competing narratives in the initial file. The managing partner blames pay, the group head blames the matter, and survey comments point to the partner. C2 alone rules out pay (H1, R3). C1 alone establishes the association between the Kestrel/Faulk exposure and resignation (R1 and R2 move from unknown to association-only). It also shows the two exposures coincide perfectly, which keeps H2 and H3 unknown. Every other plausible request is deliberately non-discriminating. C4 has no heavy-hours team without Faulk. C6 gives split reasons. C5 and C14 are interested or mention both factors. C3, C9 and C15 are blind to matter. C12 confirms Faulk leads both phases. Items that might have leaked the association (client remarks on turnover, Faulk referring to 'the same leavers', farewell emails naming Kestrel) were removed so C1 stays non-redundant. A3 and A4 are each tied to one live hypothesis and are reversible, so they are premature. The January 2027 phase change stops either of them working as a clean test. A2 is harmful because it spends on a contradicted cause and closes the review under both live hypotheses.
